claims.text: The additively manufactured Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy contains dual nanoprecipitates.
APT comparison before and after high-temperature oxidation will reveal nanoscale elemental redistribution in the nanoprecipitates.
Elemental redistribution in the dual nanoprecipitates is responsible for oxidation-related degradation.
Nanoscale elemental redistribution will illuminate mechanistic pathways governing the alloy's high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Exposure at 900–1100 °C for varying durations in an oxidizing environment will induce oxidation.
The oxidation experiment will use fixed oxygen partial pressure while systematically varying exposure temperature and time.
The nanoscale composition and morphology of nanoprecipitates can influence protective oxide-layer formation and growth.
APT with site-specific FIB specimen preparation can provide near-atomic-scale three-dimensional elemental maps.
APT maps can reveal diffusion pathways and compositional changes at and around nanoprecipitates during oxidation.
Oxidized specimens will exhibit localized elemental segregation or depletion detectable by APT.
Observed segregation or depletion patterns will clarify the role of nanoprecipitates in forming stable oxide scales.
The resulting information could guide alloy-design strategies for improved high-temperature performance.
Conventional SEM/EDS and XRD have limited spatial resolution for this application.
Conventional SEM/EDS and XRD cannot directly resolve nanometer-scale elemental distributions within the precipitates.
Operational conditions outside the tested temperature range and environment may alter oxidation and diffusion phenomena.
Failure to observe changes in nanoprecipitate partitioning or a correlation with oxidation resistance would leave the hypothesis unsupported.
